paragraphs: Now suppose the opposite arrangement, in which the provincial governments are given the power to regulate those same affairs of mixed interest. Society then leans the other way. The stronger force sits in the province rather than in the nation, and it is to be feared that the national government may in the end be stripped of the privileges it needs in order to exist.
Independent nations, then, naturally tend toward centralization, and confederations naturally tend toward dismemberment.

All that remains is to apply these general principles to the American Union. The several States necessarily held the right to regulate every affair that is purely provincial. They also kept the right to decide who is competent to act as a citizen in civil and political matters, to regulate the relations of the members of the community with one another, and to dispense justice. These rights are general in nature, yet they do not necessarily belong to a national government. We have seen that the government of the Union has the power to act in the name of the whole nation when the nation must appear as a single, undivided power: in foreign relations, for instance, and in joint resistance to a common enemy. In short, it handles the affairs I have called exclusively national.

At first glance, the Union seems to hold a larger share of sovereignty than the States do. A closer look shows that it holds a smaller one. The Union’s undertakings are more vast, but its influence is felt less often. The provincial governments’ undertakings are comparatively small, but they never stop, and they keep alive the authority behind them. The government of the Union looks after the general interests of the country. Yet the general interests of a people have a very doubtful effect on individual happiness, whereas provincial interests bear immediately on the well-being of the inhabitants. The Union secures the independence and greatness of the nation, which private citizens do not feel directly. The several States, by contrast, preserve each citizen’s liberty, regulate his rights, protect his property, and secure his life and his whole future prosperity.

The federal government stands very far from the people it governs, while the provincial governments are within everyone’s reach and ready to hear the smallest appeal. The central government has behind it the passions of a few superior men who aspire to run it. The provincial governments have behind them the interests of all the second-rate men who can hope for power only inside their own State. These men nevertheless hold the largest share of authority over the people, because they stand closest to the people’s own level. So the Americans have much more to hope for and to fear from the States than from the Union, and, following the natural bent of the human mind, they are more likely to attach themselves to the former than to the latter. On this point their habits and feelings agree with their interests.

Suppose a compact nation divides its sovereignty and adopts a confederate form of government. For a long time the people’s traditions, habits, and mores will conflict with their laws, and those traditions and habits will tend to give the central government more influence than the laws allow it. Now suppose several confederate states unite to form a single nation. The same causes then work in the opposite direction. I have no doubt that if France became a confederate republic like the United States, its government would at first show more energy than the government of the Union does. And if the Union changed its constitution to a monarchy like the French one, I think the American government would need a long time to gain the force that now governs France. When the Anglo-Americans began their national existence, their provincial existence was already old. Necessary ties had formed between the townships and between the individual citizens of each State. The people were used to treating some matters as common to all, and to handling other affairs as concerning only their own particular interests.

The Union is a vast body, and it gives patriotic feeling no definite object to attach to. The State, by contrast, has distinct and limited forms and boundaries. It stands for a certain number of things that its citizens know well and that everyone loves. It is bound up with the soil itself, with the right of property and the affections of home, with the memories of the past, the labors of the present, and the hopes of the future. Patriotism is often only individual egotism extended, and it still turns toward the State; the Union does not arouse it. Thus the interests, habits, and feelings of the people all tend to center political activity in the States rather than in the Union.

One can easily measure the relative strength of the two governments by watching how each performs its functions. When the government of a State has to speak to an individual or to a gathering of individuals, its language is clear and commanding. The federal government uses the same tone with individuals. But as soon as it has any business with a State, it starts to parley. It explains its motives and justifies its conduct, argues and advises, and does anything except command. If doubts arise over the limits of each government’s constitutional powers, the provincial government states its claim boldly and takes quick, vigorous steps to back it up. The government of the Union, meanwhile, reasons. It appeals to the nation’s interests, its good sense, and its glory; it stalls and negotiates, and it will not agree to act until it is driven to the last extremity. At first sight one might easily suppose that the provincial government is the one armed with the nation’s authority, and that Congress speaks for a single State.

The federal government is therefore, whatever precautions its founders took, so weak by nature that it particularly requires the free consent of the governed in order to survive. It is easy to see that its purpose is to help the States carry out, without difficulty, their resolve to stay united. As long as that resolve exists, its authority is great, moderate, and effective. The Constitution equips the government to control individuals and to overcome without trouble whatever obstacles they may try to put in its way. It was by no means established with the possible separation of one or more States from the Union in view.

Suppose the sovereignty of the Union entered into a struggle with that of the States today. One can confidently predict that the Union would lose, and a struggle of that kind is unlikely ever to be seriously attempted. Whenever the federal government meets steady resistance, it gives way. Experience so far shows that a State that has demanded something with perseverance and resolution has always got it, and that when a separate government has plainly refused to act, it has been left to do as it saw fit. *z

z [ See the conduct of the Northern States in the war of 1812. “During that war,” says Jefferson in a letter to General Lafayette, “four of the Eastern States were only attached to the Union, like so many inanimate bodies to living men.”]

Even if the government of the Union had some strength of its own, the physical situation of the country would make that strength hard to use. *a The United States covers an immense territory. Great distances separate the States from one another, and the population is scattered across a country that is still half wilderness. If the Union tried to compel the confederate States to obey by force of arms, it would find itself in a position much like England’s during the War of Independence.

a [ The profound peace of the Union gives no pretext for a standing army; and without a standing army a government is not prepared to take advantage of a favorable opportunity to overcome resistance and seize the sovereign power by surprise. [The results of the Civil War have shown that this note, and the paragraph in the text that precedes it, were a misconception on the writer’s part.]]

No government, however strong, can easily escape the consequences of a principle it has once accepted as the foundation of its constitution. The States formed the Union by voluntary agreement. In uniting, they did not give up their nationality, and they were not reduced to being one and the same people. If one State chose to withdraw from the contract, it would be hard to disprove its right to do so, and the federal government would have no direct way to uphold its claims, whether by force or by right. For the federal government to overcome easily the resistance of any one of its members, one or more of the others would have to have a special stake in the existence of the Union. That has often been the case in the history of confederations.

Suppose that among the States joined by the federal tie, some alone enjoy the main advantages of union, or depend for their prosperity on its lasting. It is certain that these States will always be ready to back the central government when it forces the others to obey. But the government would then be using a force that does not come from itself, and that comes instead from a principle contrary to its nature. States form confederations in order to gain equal advantages from union. In the case just described, the federal government would draw its power from the unequal distribution of those advantages among the States.

Suppose one of the confederate States has gained such a preponderance that it can take exclusive possession of the central authority. It will then treat the other States as subject provinces and will have its own supremacy respected under the borrowed name of the sovereignty of the Union. Great things may be done in the name of the federal government, but in reality that government will have ceased to exist. *b In both cases, the power acting in the confederation’s name grows stronger the further it departs from the natural state and the accepted principles of confederations.

b [ Thus the province of Holland in the republic of the Low Countries, and the Emperor in the Germanic Confederation, have sometimes put themselves in the place of the union and used the federal authority to their own advantage.]

In America the existing Union benefits every State, but it is not indispensable to any one of them. Several of them could break the federal tie without harming the welfare of the rest, though their own prosperity would suffer. The existence and happiness of none of them depend wholly on the present Constitution, so none of them would be inclined to make great personal sacrifices to preserve it. On the other hand, no State seems so far to have its ambition much bound up with keeping the existing Union in being. They certainly do not all have equal influence in the federal councils, but none can hope to lord it over the others or to treat them as inferiors or subjects.

I find it beyond doubt that if any part of the Union seriously wanted to separate from the other States, the rest could not stop it, and indeed would not try. The present Union will last only as long as the States that make it up choose to remain in the confederation. Once this point is granted, the question becomes less difficult. We are not asking whether the States of the existing Union are able to separate. We are asking whether they will choose to stay united.

Of the many reasons that make the existing Union useful to the Americans, two principal ones stand out to an observer. The Americans are, in a sense, alone on their continent, yet their trade makes them neighbors of every nation they deal with. Their isolation is only apparent. They need a certain degree of strength, and they can keep it only by staying united with one another. If the States were to split apart, they would not only reduce the strength they can now show toward foreign nations; they would soon create foreign powers on their own soil. Inland customs barriers would go up, imaginary boundary lines would cut across the valleys, territorial distinctions would restrict the courses of the rivers, and countless hindrances would keep the Americans from exploring the whole of the vast continent that Providence has given them to rule. For now they have no invasion to fear, and so they have no standing armies to maintain and no taxes to levy. If the Union dissolved, all these burdensome measures might soon be required. The Americans therefore have a very strong interest in keeping their Union. On the other hand, one can hardly find any material interest that would now tempt a part of the Union to break away from the rest.

Looking at a map of the United States, we see the chain of the Alleghany Mountains running from northeast to southwest across nearly a thousand miles of country. We are tempted to think Providence meant to raise between the valley of the Mississippi and the Atlantic coast one of those natural barriers that cut off contact between peoples and mark the necessary limits of different States. But the Alleghanies average no more than 2,500 feet in height, and their highest point is not above 4,000 feet. Their rounded summits, and the broad valleys hidden in their passes, can be entered easily from several sides. Besides this, the principal rivers that empty into the Atlantic Ocean — the Hudson, the Susquehanna, and the Potomac — all begin beyond the Alleghanies, in an open district that borders the valley of the Mississippi. They leave that region and break through the barrier that seems to turn them westward, and as they wind through the mountains they give people an easy, natural way across. There is no natural barrier anywhere in the regions the Anglo-Americans now inhabit. The Alleghanies, far from separating nations, do not even serve as a frontier between States. New York, Pennsylvania, and Virginia take them within their borders, and those States reach as far west of the line as east of it. The territory now held by the twenty-four States of the Union, together with the three great districts that already have inhabitants but have not yet been given the rank of States, covers 1,002,600 square miles, *c which is about five times the size of France. Within these limits the soil, the temperature, and the produce of the country vary enormously. The great extent of territory held by the Anglo-American republics has raised doubts about whether their Union can last. Here we must draw a distinction. In a vast empire, opposing interests sometimes arise in different provinces and often end in open conflict, and then the size of the country does the greatest harm to the power of the State. But if the inhabitants of such vast regions are not divided by opposing interests, the size of the territory may help their prosperity. Unity of government encourages the exchange of the soil’s different products, and it raises their value by making them easier to consume.

c [ See “Darby’s View of the United States,” p. 435. [In 1890 the number of States and Territories had increased to 51, the population to 62,831,900, and the area of the States to 3,602,990 square miles. This does not include the Philippine Islands, Hawaii, or Porto Rico. A conservative estimate of the population of the Philippine Islands is 8,000,000; that of Hawaii, by the census of 1897, was given as 109,020; and the present estimated population of Porto Rico is 900,000. The area of the Philippine Islands is about 120,000 square miles, that of Hawaii is 6,740 square miles, and the area of Porto Rico is about 3,600 square miles.]]

Different interests are indeed easy to find in the different parts of the Union, but I know of none that are hostile to one another. The Southern States are almost wholly agricultural. The Northern States are especially commercial and manufacturing. The Western States are agricultural and manufacturing at once. In the South the crops are tobacco, rice, cotton, and sugar; in the North and West they are wheat and maize. These are different sources of wealth, but union is the means that opens them all to everyone and makes each equally profitable to every district.

The North carries the produce of the Anglo-Americans to every part of the world and brings the world’s produce back to the Union. It plainly has an interest in keeping the confederation as it now stands, so that the number of American producers and consumers stays as large as possible. The North is the most natural go-between linking the South and West of the Union with the rest of the world. It therefore has an interest in the union and prosperity of the South and West, so that they may keep supplying raw materials for its factories and cargoes for its ships.

The South and the West, for their part, have an even more direct interest in preserving the Union and in the North’s prosperity. Most of the South’s produce is shipped overseas, so the South and the West both depend on the North’s commercial resources. They also have an interest in the Union keeping a powerful fleet to protect them effectively. The South and West own no ships, but they cannot refuse to pay willingly toward the navy’s expenses. If the fleets of Europe blockaded the ports of the South and the mouth of the Mississippi, what would become of the rice of the Carolinas, the tobacco of Virginia, and the sugar and cotton grown in the Mississippi valley? Every part of the federal budget thus helps to maintain material interests shared by all the confederate States.

Besides this commercial usefulness, the South and the West gain great political advantages from their connection with the North. The South has an enormous slave population, one that is already alarming and will be more formidable still in the future. The Western States lie at the far end of a single valley. All the rivers that cross their territory rise in the Rocky Mountains or the Alleghanies and flow into the Mississippi, which carries them on to the Gulf of Mexico. Their position therefore cuts the Western States off entirely from the traditions of Europe and the civilization of the Old World. So the people of the South have reason to support the Union in order to have its protection against Black people. The people of the West have reason to support it so as not to lose free communication with the rest of the world and be shut up in the wilds of central America. And the North cannot help wanting the Union kept in being, so that it can remain, as it is now, the link between that vast body and the rest of the world.
The material interests of all the parts of the Union, then, are closely tied together. The same is true of those opinions and feelings that may be called the immaterial interests of men.

The people of the United States talk a great deal about their love of country. I confess that I do not rely on that calculating patriotism, which rests on interest and which a change in the interests at stake can wipe out. Nor do I give much weight to the Americans’ words when, in daily conversation, they declare their intention to maintain the federal system their forefathers adopted. A government holds its sway over a great number of citizens far less through the voluntary, reasoned consent of the multitude than through an instinctive and, to some extent, involuntary agreement that comes from similar feelings and resemblances of opinion. I will never grant that men form a social body merely because they obey the same head and the same laws. Society can exist only when a great number of men see a great number of things from the same point of view, hold the same opinions on many subjects, and have the same thoughts and impressions suggested to them by the same events.

An observer who examines the present condition of the United States by this principle will readily see that, although the citizens are divided into twenty-four distinct sovereignties, they still form a single people. He may perhaps be led to think that the Anglo-American Union is more truly a society than certain nations of Europe that live under the same laws and the same prince.

The Anglo-Americans belong to several religious sects, yet they all look at religion in the same way. They do not always agree about which measures best serve good government, and they differ over some of the forms of government worth adopting. But they are unanimous about the general principles that should govern human society. From Maine to the Floridas, and from the Missouri to the Atlantic Ocean, the people is held to be the legitimate source of all power. Everywhere the same ideas are held about liberty and equality, the liberty of the press, the right of association, trial by jury, and the responsibility of the agents of government.

If we leave their political and religious opinions and turn to the moral and philosophical principles that shape the actions of daily life and guide their conduct, we find the same uniformity. The Anglo-Americans *d recognize the absolute moral authority of the community’s reason, just as they recognize the political authority of the mass of citizens, and they hold that public opinion is the surest judge of what is allowed or forbidden, true or false. Most of them believe that a man will be led to do what is just and good by following his own self-interest properly understood. They hold that every man is born with the right to govern himself, and that no one has the right to force his fellow creatures to be happy. They all have a lively faith in human perfectibility. They think that the spread of knowledge must have good effects and that ignorance must have fatal ones. They all see society as a body that is improving, and humanity as a changing scene in which nothing is, or should be, permanent. And they admit that what seems good to them today may be replaced tomorrow by something better. I do not offer all these opinions as true. I cite them as characteristic of the Americans.

d [ I hardly need point out that by the expression Anglo-Americans I mean only the great majority of the nation; for a certain number of isolated individuals are of course to be found holding very different opinions.]

These shared opinions are not all that unites the Anglo-Americans. A common feeling of pride also sets them apart from every other nation. For the last fifty years, no effort has been spared to persuade the people of the United States that they alone are religious, enlightened, and free. They see that for the moment their own democratic institutions succeed while those of other countries fail. They therefore form an inflated opinion of their own superiority, and they are not far from believing that they belong to a different race of mankind.

The dangers that threaten the American Union come not from diversity of interests or opinions but from the differing characters and passions of the Americans. The men who live across the vast territory of the United States are almost all descended from one common stock. But climate, and above all slavery, have gradually produced very striking differences between the British settler in the Southern States and the British settler in the North. In Europe it is generally believed that slavery has set the interests of one part of the Union against those of another. I did not find this to be so at all. Slavery has not created interests in the South opposed to those of the North. What it has done is change the character and habits of the South’s native-born people.

I have already explained how slavery has affected the commercial ability of the Southern Americans, and the same influence extends equally to their mores. The slave is a servant who never protests and who submits to everything without complaint. He may sometimes murder his master, but he never stands up to him. In the South no family is too poor to own slaves. From his earliest years the Southern citizen holds a kind of domestic dictatorship. The first idea he gets in life is that he was born to command, and the first habit he forms is that of being obeyed without resistance. His upbringing thus tends to make him haughty and hasty: irascible, violent, and ardent in his desires, impatient with obstacles, yet easily discouraged if he fails at his first attempt.

The American of the Northern States grows up with no slaves around him, and not even free servants to wait on him, and he usually has to provide for his own needs. As soon as he enters the world, the idea of necessity presses on him from every side. He quickly learns exactly where the natural limit of his authority lies. He never expects to subdue by force those who resist him, and he knows that the surest way to win the support of his fellow creatures is to earn their favor. So he becomes patient, thoughtful, tolerant, slow to act, and steady in his plans.

In the Southern States the more pressing needs of life are always provided for. The people there are not occupied with the material cares of life, since others always attend to them, and their imagination turns to more captivating and less definite objects. The Southerner loves grandeur, luxury, and renown, gaiety and pleasure, and above all idleness. Nothing forces him to exert himself to make a living, and since he has no necessary occupation, he gives in to laziness and does not even try what would be useful.

In the North, however, equality of fortunes and the absence of slavery plunge people into the same cares of daily life that the white population of the South looks down on. From infancy they are taught to fight want and to put comfort above every pleasure of the mind or heart. Imagination is stifled by the petty details of life, and ideas grow fewer and less general, though far more practical and precise. Since prosperity is the only aim of their efforts, they reach it superbly. Nature and mankind are turned to the best financial account, and society is cleverly made to serve the welfare of each of its members, so that individual egotism becomes the source of general happiness.

The Northerner has not only experience but knowledge, and yet he values the pleasures of knowledge very little. To him it is a means to an end, and he is eager only to seize its most profitable uses. The Southerner is more inclined to act on impulse. He is cleverer, more open, more generous, more intellectual, and more brilliant. The Northerner has more activity, common sense, information, and general ability, and he has the characteristic virtues and vices of the middle classes. The Southerner has the tastes, prejudices, weaknesses, and magnanimity of every aristocracy. Take two men who share a society and have the same interests and, to some degree, the same opinions, but who differ in character, in what they have learned, and in their style of civilization. They will probably not agree. The same holds for a society of nations. Slavery, then, does not attack the American Union directly through its interests, but indirectly through its mores.

Thirteen States gave their assent to the federal contract in 1790. The Union now has thirty-four members. The population, nearly 4,000,000 in 1790, more than tripled in forty years and reached nearly 13,000,000 in 1830. *e Changes on this scale cannot take place without some danger.

A society of nations, like a society of individuals, owes its main chances of lasting to the wisdom of its members, their individual weakness, and their small number. The Americans who leave the Atlantic coast and plunge into the western wilderness are adventurers who cannot bear restraint, who are greedy for wealth, and who are often men driven out of the States where they were born. When they reach the wilds, they are strangers to one another, and they have no traditions, no family feeling, and no example to hold their excesses in check. Among them the rule of law is weak, and that of morality weaker still. The settlers who keep filling the Mississippi valley are thus in every respect far inferior to the Americans of the older parts of the Union. Yet they already have great influence in its councils, and they come to govern the commonwealth before they have learned to govern themselves. *f
f [ This is indeed only a temporary danger. I have no doubt that in time society will acquire as much stability and regularity in the West as it already has on the coast of the Atlantic Ocean.]

The weaker each party to a contract is individually, the better the chances that the contract will last, since their safety then depends on staying united. In 1790 the most populous of the American republics had fewer than 500,000 inhabitants. *g Each felt how insignificant it was as an independent people, and that feeling made it easier to comply with the federal authority. But consider a confederate State like New York, which counts 2,000,000 inhabitants and covers a territory equal to a quarter of France. *h Such a State feels its own strength. It may keep supporting the Union because the Union helps its prosperity, but it no longer sees the Union as necessary to its existence. And while it remains a party to the federal compact, it soon aims at preponderance in the federal assemblies. The likelihood of unanimity among the States diminishes as their number grows. Today the interests of the different parts of the Union do not conflict. But who can foresee the many changes still to come in a country where towns are founded from one day to the next, and States almost from one year to the next?
g [ Pennsylvania contained 431,373 inhabitants in 1790 [and 5,258,014 in 1890.]]
h [ The area of the State of New York is 49,170 square miles. [See U. S. census report of 1890.]]

Ever since the British colonies were first settled, their population has roughly doubled every twenty-two years. I can see nothing likely to halt this steady growth of the Anglo-American population during the next hundred years. Before that time is up, I believe, the territories and dependencies of the United States will hold more than 100,000,000 inhabitants and be divided into forty States. *i I grant that these 100,000,000 men will have no hostile interests. I even suppose that they all have an equal stake in keeping the Union. Still, I hold that with 100,000,000 men and forty distinct nations of unequal strength, the survival of the federal government can only be a lucky accident.

i [ If the population continues to double every twenty-two years, as it has done for the last two hundred years, the number of inhabitants in the United States in 1852 will be twenty millions; in 1874, forty-eight millions; and in 1896, ninety-six millions. This may still be the case even if the lands on the western slope of the Rocky Mountains turn out to be unfit for cultivation. The territory already occupied can easily hold this number of inhabitants. One hundred millions of men spread over the surface of the twenty-four States and the three dependencies that make up the Union would give only 762 inhabitants to the square league. This is far below the mean population of France, which is 1,063 to the square league, or of England, which is 1,457; and it would even be below the population of Switzerland, for that country, despite its lakes and mountains, has 783 inhabitants to the square league. See “Malte Brun,” vol. vi. p. 92.

[The actual result has fallen somewhat short of these calculations, despite the vast territorial acquisitions of the United States; but in 1899 the population is probably about eighty-seven millions, including the population of the Philippines, Hawaii, and Porto Rico.]]

However much faith I have in human perfectibility, I will refuse to believe that a government can last when it is asked to hold together forty different peoples spread over a territory half the size of Europe, to prevent all rivalry, ambition, and conflict among them, and to direct their independent activity toward the same ends. I will keep refusing until human nature changes and men are wholly transformed.

But the greatest danger the Union faces from its growth comes from the constant shifting of its internal strength. From Lake Superior to the Gulf of Mexico the distance runs from the 47th to the 30th degree of latitude, more than 1,200 miles in a straight line. The frontier of the United States winds along this whole immense line, sometimes falling inside it, but more often reaching far beyond it into the wilderness. It has been calculated that the whites advance an average of seventeen miles a year along this entire vast boundary. *j Now and then they meet obstacles: an unproductive district, a lake, or a Native American nation they did not expect to find. The advancing column then halts for a while. Its two ends fall back on themselves, and as soon as they have joined up again, they move forward. This slow, unbroken progress of the European race toward the Rocky Mountains has the solemnity of a providential event. It is like a flood of men that keeps rising and is driven forward every day by the hand of God.
j [ See Legislative Documents, 20th Congress, No. 117, p. 105.]

Within this first line of conquering settlers, towns are built and great States founded. In 1790 only a few thousand pioneers were scattered along the valleys of the Mississippi. Today those valleys hold as many people as the entire Union held in 1790. Their population is nearly 4,000,000. *k The city of Washington was founded in 1800 at the very center of the Union. But so much has changed that it now lies at one of the extremities, and the delegates from the most remote Western States already have to make a journey as long as the one from Vienna to Paris. *l
l [ The distance from Jefferson, the capital of the State of Missouri, to Washington is 1,019 miles. (“American Almanac,” 1831, p. 48.)]

All the States are carried forward together along the road to fortune, but they naturally do not all grow and prosper at the same rate. In the North, the outlying branches of the Alleghany chain run all the way to the Atlantic Ocean and form spacious roadsteads and ports that vessels of the greatest burden can always enter. But from the Potomac to the mouth of the Mississippi the coast is sandy and flat. In this part of the Union the mouths of nearly all the rivers are blocked, and the few harbors among the lagoons offer ships much shallower water and far fewer commercial advantages than those of the North.
